title: 1. Cattle preferential intake of seaweed supplementation and effects on methane emissions.
content:
Abstract
Seaweed contains halogenated compounds, such as phlorotannins and bromoforms, that directly affect the methanogenesis pathway, reducing cattle enteric CH4 by disrupting microbial metabolism. Pacific Dulse or Dulse (Devaleraea mollis), is a fast-growing red macroalga that has been considered as potential CH4 mitigator. However, information on supplementation of cattle with Dulse is limited, and palatability of such supplement has not been investigated. Therefore, the objective of this study was to evaluate the preferential intake of cattle offered Dulse supplementation mixed with dry distiller’s grains (DDG) at different concentrations. Ten mature beef cows (Angus x Hereford, 501 ± 12 kg) were enrolled in the study. Body weight (BW) of all cows was collected before the initiation of supplementation (d-7), at the beginning (d0) and at the end the supplementation (d21), as well as a week after the end of the supplementation (d28). Methane emissions were measured using Greenfeed Pasture System for one week before supplementation (d-7 to 0), and for one week after the supplementation (d21 to 28). During CH4 measurement weeks, cows were maintained as a group in dry lot pens and had ad libitum access to alfalfa-meadow hay mix (12% CP and 59% TDN). During the supplementation phase (d0 to 21) cows were moved to individual dry lot pens and were limited fed 8 kg of the hay mix. Every morning each cow was offered three portions of DDG (226g) fortified with Dulse at three different concentrations (0.25, 0.50, and 1% of total dry matter intake). Cows had free and simultaneous access to the fortified supplements for 4h before the hay feeding. Supplement refusals were weighed daily after the 4h period to determine preferential intake of the supplement. Preliminary data were analyzed using a MIXED procedure of SAS with time (pre- and post-supplementation) as a fixed effect and cow as the experimental unit. As expected with the limited feeding strategy adopted, cows fully consumed the hay offered daily. No preferences were observed for any of the Dulse concentrations used to fortify the DDG supplement. In fact, cows completely consumed all the supplement offered in the 4h interval, resulting in a daily intake of 150g of Dulse. Regardless of the limited feeding strategy, cows had greater BW at the end of the supplementation phase (P < 0.01; 501 vs. 519) and tended to have reduced CH4 emissions after the supplementation phase (P = 0.09; 181 vs. 170 ± 6 g/cow daily, for pre and post supplementation, respectively). These preliminary results indicate that Dulse supplementation was readily accepted by cattle and showed potential to reduce enteric CH4 emissions, warranting further investigation under longer supplementation periods and larger sample sizes.
